title: Gratitude, again
hook: gratitude of heart, tongue and limbs

segments.voice: Yesterday, patience, and your line: three patiences. When your chosen test came, did you give it the first moment? Today, the station that walks beside patience. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

Cracked feet. That's the detail his wife Aisha remembers: the Prophet ﷺ would stand in prayer at night so long that his feet cracked. And she asks the obvious question. Why do this, when Allah has already forgiven you, past and future? It's a fair question. If the reason for prayer were fear of punishment, he'd have no reason to stand. His answer, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, turns the whole thing over. Should I not be a grateful servant? He isn't standing to earn something. He's standing to thank someone. Today, gratitude that reaches all the way to the feet.
screen: `FEET CRACKED FROM STANDING.` → `WHY, IF YOU'RE FORGIVEN?` → `SHOULD I NOT BE GRATEFUL?`

segments.voice: Gratitude in Arabic is shukr. Al-Ghazali, in the Revival, says it isn't one act but works through the whole person, and he names three places it lives. First, the heart. Gratitude of the heart is knowing where the gift came from. Not luck, not only your own effort, but Allah behind the hands that brought it. Second, the tongue. Saying it out loud. Alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, is the plainest form. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, in Pickthall's translation: "Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse." Talk about the good you've been given. Third, the limbs. Using a gift in a way the giver would love. Eyes used to see kindly. Hands used to help. Strength used to stand at night, the way the Prophet did. In the Qur'an, the family of David is told to work in gratitude, so the work itself becomes the thanks. You can see why al-Ghazali needs all three. Thanks in the heart alone stays private. Thanks on the tongue alone can be a reflex, like a thank-you said without looking up. Thanks in the limbs alone can become a list of chores. Put together, it's one motion: I know it's a gift, I say so, and I use it well. And there's a promise attached, in Pickthall's words: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Patience, yesterday, was holding steady when it's hard. Gratitude is what the same heart does when it's good.
screen: `THE HEART: KNOW WHERE IT CAME FROM.` · `THE TONGUE: SAY IT ALOUD.` · `THE LIMBS: USE IT WELL.` · then, large: `IF YE GIVE THANKS, I WILL GIVE YOU MORE.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank in all three ways, for one thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose one good thing in your life right now. Your hands are a fine choice, or a person, or the room you're in. First the heart: hold it in mind and let yourself know it's a gift, not something you're owed. Then the tongue: say quietly, thank you, or if you pray, alhamdulillah. Then the limbs: decide one way you'll use that very gift today for something good. Hands that will help carry something. A voice that will call someone. The bell holds the time.
Gratitude. Shukr: thanks with the heart that knows the giver, the tongue that says so, and the limbs that use the gift well. Today's word.
Your line: thanks with all of me. Today, carry out the one use you chose, and when you've done it, say thank you again. Tomorrow, reliance after effort. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Muslims say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, throughout the day, after meals, on waking and when asked how they are, and teachers describe gratitude as reaching the heart, the tongue and the deeds of the body.

fork.setup: you're Aisha. it's night, and the Prophet ﷺ has stood in prayer so long his feet are cracked. you ask why, since he is already forgiven. what does he answer?

the night is when prayers are answered.
fork.reveal: in Sahih al-Bukhari, he says: should I not be a grateful servant? the standing was thanks, not payment.
